questions.question: Stars are born inside nebulae, vast clouds of gas and dust, but only in their coldest, densest clumps, at about 260 degrees below zero Celsius. There a clump falls in on itself and becomes a star, while the warmer gas around it does not. Why do stars form in the cold clumps?
questions.answer: Cold gas pushes back too weakly to resist gravity
choices: Cold gas pushes back too weakly to resist gravity
Gas gains extra gravity as it cools down
Cold gas is pulled together by the nebula's magnetism
Cold gas is drawn in by the gravity of nearby stars
questions.context: Gravity pulls a clump of a nebula inward while the heat in its gas pushes outward, and the warmer the gas, the harder it pushes. In the coldest, densest clumps the push is too weak, so gravity wins and the clump collapses into a protostar, which heats up as it shrinks. Gravity depends on mass, not on temperature, and a nebula's magnetism helps hold its gas up against collapse rather than pulling it together.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) begins a star's life cycle with gravity pulling a nebula's gas and dust together into a protostar.

questions.question: A star of 16 Suns' mass is born with far more fuel than the Sun. Yet the Sun will shine for about ten billion years, and the bigger star for only about ten million. Why does the bigger star burn out so much sooner?
questions.answer: Its hotter core burns its fuel far faster
choices: Its hotter core burns its fuel far faster
Its bigger surface burns its fuel far faster
Its gravity crushes it before its fuel runs out
Its fuel is a kind that burns away faster
questions.context: A heavier star needs more pressure in its core to hold up its weight, so its core is hotter, and a hotter core burns fuel enormously faster. The 16-Sun star has about 16 times the Sun's fuel but burns it thousands of times faster, so it lasts about a thousandth as long. A star burns its fuel only in its core, never at its surface, the two stars burn the same fuel, and a star's core collapses only after its fuel is spent.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) teaches that a star's mass decides its life cycle, the massive stars living fast and dying young.

questions.question: William Herschel named round, glowing clouds like the Ring Nebula 'planetary nebulae', because in his telescope they looked like the discs of planets. A tiny, white-hot star shines at the Ring Nebula's centre. What is the glowing ring?
questions.answer: Gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star
choices: Gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star
Gas and dust where new planets are forming
Gas and dust where new stars are being born
Gas blasted out when a massive star exploded
questions.context: Near the end of its life a Sun-like star swells into a red giant, then puffs its outer layers off into space. That glowing shell is a planetary nebula, and the hot core left in the middle is a white dwarf about the size of Earth; the Sun will end this way. Herschel's name stuck, but planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets, and a massive star ends instead in a supernova blast.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) teaches the Sun-like star's path: main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf.

questions.question: Two of the brightest stars in Orion are supergiants, both far larger and brighter than the Sun. Betelgeuse, at the hunter's shoulder, glows orange-red, and Rigel, at his foot, shines blue-white. What do their colours show?
questions.answer: Rigel's surface is far hotter than Betelgeuse's
choices: Rigel's surface is far hotter than Betelgeuse's
Betelgeuse's surface is far hotter than Rigel's
Rigel is far closer to Earth than Betelgeuse
Rigel is far larger than Betelgeuse
questions.context: A star's colour shows its surface temperature: the hotter the surface, the more of its light is blue. Rigel's surface is about 12,100 kelvins and Betelgeuse's about 3,500, against the Sun's 5,800. Red means a cooler star, though many people guess the reverse from the red of a fire, and Betelgeuse is in fact both the far larger star and the nearer one.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A, as taught) teaches that a star's colour shows its surface temperature: blue stars are hottest, red stars coolest.

questions.question: Ejnar Hertzsprung, a Danish astronomer, and Henry Norris Russell, at Princeton, worked separately between 1911 and 1913, plotting stars' true brightness against their surface temperature. Most stars, the Sun among them, fell into one band across the chart, the main sequence. When the Sun's core runs low on fuel, its outer layers will swell to many times their present width, and it will leave the band. How will the swollen Sun differ from the Sun of today?
choices: Brighter, with a cooler surface
Brighter, with a hotter surface
Dimmer, with a cooler surface
Dimmer, with a hotter surface
questions.context: Swelling cools the Sun's outer layers, so its surface will glow red, yet the swollen Sun will be so vast that it gives off far more light than today: it will be a red giant, which sits above the main sequence on the cool side of the chart. The band holds about nine stars in ten, running from hot, bright blue stars to cool, dim red ones, and the chart is now called the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Russell at first read the band as a path every star slides down as it ages, a picture later drastically revised, for a star's place on it is set by its mass.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) follows a Sun-like star from the main sequence to a red giant and classifies stars on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, where red giants sit above the band on its cool side.

questions.question: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, has a faint partner, Sirius B, first seen by Alvan Graham Clark in 1862. Sirius B's surface is more than four times as hot as the Sun's, yet it gives off less than a tenth as much light. Why is so hot a star so dim?
questions.answer: It is tiny, about the size of Earth
choices: It is tiny, about the size of Earth
Its strong gravity traps most of its light
Only small patches of its surface are hot
It is a newborn star, not yet fully alight
questions.context: A star's light depends on how hot its surface is and on how much surface it has. Sirius B is a white dwarf, about as much mass as the Sun packed into a ball about as big as Earth, so all of its surface glows white-hot but there is very little of it. On the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram white dwarfs sit below the main sequence on the hot side; Sirius B's gravity is strong, but it does not trap light as a black hole's does.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) compares stars on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, where white dwarfs sit hot but dim because they are so small.

questions.question: A white dwarf has no fuel left to burn. It is held up against its own gravity by its electrons, squeezed so tightly that they push back. Sailing from India to England in 1930, 19-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar set out to work out how much mass that push can hold up. As astronomers figure it today, what is the answer?
questions.answer: At most about 1.4 times the Sun's mass
choices: At most about 1.4 times the Sun's mass
At most about 14 times the Sun's mass
At most about 140 times the Sun's mass
Any mass at all, however great
questions.context: Chandrasekhar brought in Einstein's special relativity: in a heavier white dwarf the electrons are squeezed so hard that they move at nearly the speed of light, and their push can no longer keep up with gravity. His own first figure was about 0.91 Suns, because the make-up of stars was then misjudged; with the make-up now known his sums give about 1.4, and above that a dead star's core cannot settle as a white dwarf and collapses further, into a neutron star or a black hole. The older sums, without relativity, set no ceiling, and Arthur Eddington held that electron pressure could hold up any mass; the limit now carries Chandrasekhar's name.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches the white dwarf as a Sun-like star's end and a massive star's collapse to a neutron star or black hole (TEKS 8.9A); Chandrasekhar's limit is the line between them.

questions.question: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar presented his limit for white dwarfs to the Royal Astronomical Society in London in January 1935. Arthur Eddington, Britain's leading astrophysicist, spoke straight after him and attacked it: there should be a law of Nature, he said, to prevent a star from behaving in so absurd a way. What did Eddington find absurd?
questions.answer: A dead star collapsing with nothing to halt it
choices: A dead star collapsing with nothing to halt it
A dead star as small as Earth but as heavy as the Sun
A dead star blowing itself apart in a blast
A dead star swelling back up into a giant
questions.context: Chandrasekhar's sums left nothing to halt the collapse of a dead star above his limit, and Eddington, who had found how a star's brightness follows from its mass and written The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926), called that absurd, though he accepted white dwarfs themselves. Niels Bohr and Wolfgang Pauli agreed with Chandrasekhar but kept out of the quarrel in public, and Eddington never took his words back. The evidence sided with the younger man: weighed white dwarfs fall below his limit, neutron stars and black holes were found, and he shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on how stars end (TEKS 8.9A) reach the collapse to neutron stars and black holes, the result Eddington refused and the evidence bore out.

questions.question: Astronomers of China's Song dynasty recorded a 'guest star' in the summer of 1054. It shone in daylight for 23 days and stayed in the night sky for nearly two years before it faded away. Near that place in the sky now lies the Crab Nebula, a cloud of glowing gas still spreading outward. What had the astronomers seen?
questions.answer: A massive star exploding as a supernova
choices: A massive star exploding as a supernova
A Sun-like star throwing off its outer layers
A new star lighting up inside a nebula
A comet passing close to the Sun
questions.context: A supernova is the blast that ends a massive star's life, and this one blazed by day from about 6,500 light-years away. The Crab Nebula is its wreckage, still rushing outward at up to 1,500 kilometres a second, and at its heart spins what is left of the star's core, a neutron star about 20 kilometres across. A Sun-like star ends more gently, with no supernova at all.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) teaches that a massive star ends in a supernova that leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

questions.question: Jocelyn Bell, a graduate student at Cambridge, spent two years helping to build a new radio telescope. Checking its paper charts in 1967, she noticed a 'bit of scruff': radio pulses from one spot among the stars, arriving every 1.337 seconds as steadily as a clock. Her team nicknamed the source 'Little Green Men 1'. What was sending the pulses?
questions.answer: A neutron star spinning very fast
choices: A neutron star spinning very fast
A white dwarf swelling and shrinking
Two stars circling close round each other
A young star flaring as it forms
questions.context: A neutron star is the collapsed core a supernova leaves behind, more massive than the Sun yet only about 20 kilometres across, and as it turns it sweeps beams of radio waves past Earth like a lighthouse. The team's 1968 report also weighed a pulsing white dwarf; then the Crab Nebula's pulsar, found that year in the wreck of the 1054 supernova, proved too fast for any other explanation, flashing about 30 times a second. Antony Hewish, her supervisor, shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics, cited for his part in the discovery; Bell was left out.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.9A) teaches the neutron star as a massive star's remnant; Bell's pulsar of 1967 was the first one found.

8f6e6e1a90.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'Cold gas catches fire more easily than warm gas' was silly, so only three choices were live. Replaced, as the judge proposed, by the nebula's magnetism pulling the gas together, a real-sounding force that in fact resists the collapse (F27, sourced now). Stem unchanged.

9d4071711c.why: Judge (medium, tell): the stem's figures (more fuel, shorter life) made 'faster' the answer, and the key was the only choice that said it. As the judge proposed, three choices now tell a story of fast burning or early ending ('Its bigger surface burns its fuel far faster' replaces the weak cooler-core mirror, and the fuel-kind choice says 'faster'), so the core's heat must decide. The context adds that a star burns its fuel only in its core (F28). Stem unchanged.

f5b7955e9c.why: Judge (medium, tell): the key (hot, bright to cool, dim) matched everyday sense, and two choices were weak, since a band across the chart cannot keep one axis fixed; the judge also found the red giant, core scope, never keyed. The stem now teaches the main sequence and asks how the Sun will change as it swells into a red giant, as a 2x2 of brightness and surface temperature (F7, F29: the outer layers cool, the star grows far brighter). The judge's own fix (which stars sit far above the band on its cool side) was not used: its stem's 'cool' and 'much brighter' ruled out the red dwarf, white dwarf and blue supergiant choices. The stem does not name the red giant, since 'red' would give away the cooler surface; the context names it.

33edca010e.why: Fact-check (uncertain): Chandrasekhar's own first figure (1931) was about 0.91 Suns, because stars' mean molecular weight was then taken as 2.5; 1.44 came after it was revised (F30). The stem now asks the limit as astronomers figure it today and the context gives his first figure. The fact-check's wording ('What is that limit...') was not used: 'limit' would rule out the 'Any mass at all' choice, so the stem asks for 'the answer'. Key and choices unchanged.

69874dc35d.why: Fact-check (uncertain, context): the motive 'given Eddington's standing' for Bohr's and Pauli's public silence is not agreed (Wikipedia: his status; MacTutor: they said they were too busy), so it is dropped: they 'kept out of the quarrel in public' (F31). Judge (low, stance): to be fair to Eddington the context now names his own work on the insides of stars, the mass-luminosity relation and his 1926 book (F32). Stem and choices unchanged.
